newsitem.title: USA: Traders surprised by bullish stockpile cobalt sale.
newsitem.headline: Traders surprised by bullish stockpile cobalt sale.

text.p: U.S. cobalt traders said they were surprised by the outcome of the U.S. government's stockpile sale where only a fraction of the available metal was awarded to just one company, with many of the remaining bids dismissed.
Glencore Limited, Conn. part of Swiss-based Glencore International, was awarded 200,806 pounds of contained metal for a total of $3,910,231 on Wednesday.
The company bought 107,897 pounds of 99.00 to 99.29 percent grade cobalt at $19.01 per pound, with rest of the award at $20.01 per pound for 99.30 to 99.39 percent grade metal.
The stockpile said several bidders failed to comply with the terms and conditions of the invitation to bid for a million pounds of metal.
The global cobalt market had been awaiting the outcome of the sale. The stockpile has the same clout as a significantly sized producer in the market.
Stockpile administrator Richard Connelly said several of the bidders had not specified which category they were bidding for in the new forms.
However, one dealer noted that F&S International and Powmet both offered a higher price per cobalt unit for material than was eventually awarded to Glencore.
"They blew it by not awarding F&S and Powmet who have an unbelieveable legitimacy to appeal," the dealer said. "They literally gave away $50,000."
The dealer estimated that, based on the unit price per pound of contained cobalt in the higher grade, the stockpile should not have sold the lower grade metal for less than $19.90 per pound.
Connelly confirmed that Powmet and F&S had submitted their bids correctly.
"Glencore won for the lower price for 99.02 and 99.05 grade material with a high nickel content. F&S and Powmet bid on higher graded contained material with lower impurity levels," Connelly said.
"So we made a judgement call, and as usual, judgement calls are open to second guessing," he said, adding "I cannot change it now."
Connelly said that for the higher grade 99.3 percent material, Glencore was paying more than $20 per pound for the "same kind of stuff F&S and Powmet were bidding at 50 cents lower."
One trader whose bid failed to win, said: "I am surprised that if their goal was revenue, that they did not accept the higher bids as well."
Nevertheless the outcome was considered bullish by traders and pushed up the market price by at least 25 cents per pound Wednesday.
Only 91 tonnes will hit the market instead of a possible 453 tonnes if all the available metal had been awarded, traders noted.
"I don't think this will cause a shortage, but there won't be any pressure on the part of people to sell what they have because they are worried about the competition," a trader said.
The cobalt buyer expected prices to remain stable during December with a little uptick in January before tailing off again.
Traders noted that Minor Metals, a key player and rival to Glencore in the market, was unable to get material in the tender.

"It's a feather in Glencore's cap," a buyer said. "Both their pricing in bids were not that far apart. From a philosophical point of view, they both think the market is going in the same direction, which is up," the buyer added.
The next cobalt sale by sealed bid was scheduled for March 1997. A cobalt sale by negotiation will be held in February 1997.
-- Huw Jones, New York Commodities 212-859-1646
